devices.description: Casa C100G CMTS/CCAP - 13RU, 14 paired front/rear slots. Front and rear slot N are two halves of one logical position: a DOCSIS line card in front N requires its I/O partner in rear N.

gaps.note: The BDM2/BDM2m datasheet states "Total Power 300 W" in a technical specifications table headed "BDM2/2 m with 6+12 IO Card", whose RF connector row describes that card's six downstream and twelve upstream ports. The figure is the assembly's. A BDM position is TWO modules here - casa/bdm in a front bay and casa/io-6p12 in the paired rear bay, which is why casa/bdm already carries `pairs-with` - and no document we hold divides the 300 W between them. Writing it onto the front module would make the chassis total come out right and the answer to "what does a BDM front module draw" come out wrong, so neither half carries a figure and the chassis total stays a floor. The arithmetic does not settle it either way: 12 x 300 W lands on the C100G's stated 3.6 kW whether the 300 W is the pair or the front half with small rear cards. The C100G HIG corroborates the assembly reading and hedges it: Tables A-10 and A-11 both read "Approximately 300W per BDM" under titles scoping them to the BDM WITH its 6+12 I/O. THE LIBRARY IS CURRENTLY INCONSISTENT ABOUT THIS, ON PURPOSE AND VISIBLY. The three BDM variants carry NO power figure, for the reason above. The DQM and DCU cards added later DO carry one - DS8x8 220, DS8x96 320, DS8x192 350, US16x8 220, US16x4 150 - each with a `power-scope` provenance entry saying in the vendor's own words that the number covers the card WITH its I/O module and must not have a rear figure added to it. Both are defensible readings of the same problem: one keeps the per-module answer honest and the chassis total a floor, the other keeps the vendor's only published number reachable. They should not stay different once a pairing-scoped mechanism exists, and this is the record of which way each went and why, so that whoever unifies them is not guessing. THE THREE REAR RF I/O CARDS ADDED LATER FALL ON THE SAME SIDE OF THIS AS THE 6+12. casa/rfd, casa/rfu-16x8 and casa/ups-32x4 carry NO power figure, because Tables A-8 and A-9 give their port counts and connector types and no watts at all, and every figure Casa does publish for the slot is already the pair's - Table A-3 heads the DQM column "Maximum consumption with I/O module" and Table A-4 gives "Single DCU w/ RFU I/O" 200 W against "Single DCU w/ RFU UPS 32x4 I/O" 220 W for the same US16x8. Subtracting one from the other to get a rear card's share would be our arithmetic and would also be the wrong subtraction - the 20 W is the difference between two PAIRINGS, not between two I/O cards.
gaps.wanted: a pairable unit that can carry properties, so that a figure measured on a pair can be attached to the pair. The scope is now DATA - every card here declares `power-draw-scope: module-with-paired-io`, so a chassis sum knows not to add the rear partner and L30 catches it if one gains its own figure - but the scope says only THAT the figure covers a pair, not WHICH pair. The C100G HIG gives the same US16x8 200 W with the RFU I/O and 220 W with the RFU UPS 32x4, and the manifest can carry only one of them. Asking for "a per-module figure" was the wrong question: Casa states none, and one may not exist to be divided out. What is missing is the mechanism, and enough vendors doing this to design one from - Casa is the only one in the corpus.

gaps.note: The HIG body text states "Each fan assembly module has a maximum power consumption of 100W, totaling 300W across the three fan assemblies". Table A-2 of the same guide gives the row "Fan assembly (3)" as "330W maximum, 220W typical". Both are about the set of three and 300 is not 330. The contract takes 100 W because it is the only figure stated PER MODULE, which is the granularity a bay occupant needs; dividing 330 by three would be our arithmetic, not the vendor's. A chassis total is therefore 30 W light against the guide's own set figure, and no per-module typical exists at all.
gaps.wanted: a measurement from a running chassis, a vendor erratum, or a later revision of the guide that drops one of the two figures

gaps.note: Casa rates a power ENTRY module in amps and volts, never in watts. gaps.note: The PEM band's BOTTOM edge at 264.5 is agreed by every source and is not in doubt. That argument is sound but it is an argument, not a measurement, and the whole disagreement is six pixels at 2.982 px/mm. A tape measure on a real C40G, or any Casa drawing that dimensions the rear panel, would settle it in one number. FIGURE 1-12 HAS NOW BEEN LOOKED AT AND DOES NOT SETTLE IT, recorded so nobody spends the search twice. "C40G power entry module" is the only isolated drawing of this part and the first independent look anything has had at it. Its body measures 866 x 381 px for an aspect of 2.273. The modelled 158.0 x 68.5 is 2.307 and the superseded 158.0 x 70.5 is 2.241, and 2.273 lands 0.04 percent off the midpoint of those two - at 158.0 wide it implies a height of 69.51. IT IS EQUIDISTANT AND CONFIRMS NEITHER. This guide's isolated part drawings are in any case demonstrably about 10 percent wrong about their own aspect - Figure 1-20 draws a card at 12.54 whose real aspect is 11.34 - so a 1.5 percent lean is well inside the drawing's own error. THE NUMBER IS THEREFORE NOT MOVED. It has been moved twice already, in both directions, and a third move on evidence that splits the difference would be the reconciliation loop rather than an escape from it. What Figure 1-12 does confirm is the ARRANGEMENT, which is what a figure is good for: a bolted terminal cover across the top with three fasteners, a minus pair of studs above a plus pair inside two outlined blocks, two release levers standing proud of the body top and bottom, and the yellow disconnect-power label to their right - all of which casa/c40g-pem draws. RECORDED BECAUSE THE MODULE AND THE BAY NOW AGREE, which means nothing will ever flag this again - the fit check that found the original 2 mm discrepancy is satisfied by both being wrong together as easily as by both being right.

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series ASR 9001 Router - a 2 RU fixed-port aggregation services router with an integrated route processor, four fixed 10 GE SFP+ ports, two modular port adapter bays and 120 Gbps of fabric. Everything is on the front face: both MPA bays, both power supplies, the side-mounted fan tray and every port. The rear is a plain louvred panel.

gaps.note: The ASR 9001-S is the same metal as the ASR 9001 with two of its four fixed SFP+ ports disabled until a licence is applied. That is not a population fact - the cages are physically present and identical - so `bays:` cannot express it, and the ports are correctly drawn present in both configurations. INVESTIGATED AND IT DOES NOT REACH: `component-attrs` is the closest mechanism the format has, and it is keyed by component NAME rather than by placement id. render.py computes `comp_name = ref.split("/")[-1].split("@")[0]` and looks the overrides up by that, so `component-attrs: {sfp-ganged: ...}` would mark all SIX std/sfp-ganged instances on this chassis - both CLUSTER ports and all four SFP+ - when only two are disabled. A placement can carry `attrs:` per instance but not per configuration; `component-attrs` is per configuration but not per instance. The 9001-S needs both at once and neither mechanism spans the gap. The same edge stops this configuration carrying its own 60 Gbps fabric figure, since a configuration cannot override device attrs at all.
gaps.wanted: per-instance attrs in a configuration - `component-attrs` keyed by placement id as well as by component name would do it - or a device-attrs override in a configuration. This is a second instance of the shape recorded in working/notes/config-scoped-placements.md, from a different vendor: the format can say what OCCUPIES a bay per configuration, but not what is TRUE of a part per configuration.

gaps.note: Table 4 of the fixed-port install guide gives the 10MHz and 1PPS connectors as DIN 1.0/2.3. The standards registry has no key for it - sma, smb, mcx and f-type are there, DIN 1.0/2.3 is not - so these two openings are declared as panel cutouts at their measured size rather than composed from a std/ part. Substituting sma or smb would name a connector Cisco does not. THE REASON WAS vendor-silent AND THAT WAS THE WRONG TOKEN. Cisco is not silent - it names the connector outright. What is missing is a panel-cutout dimension, which is needs-drawing, and the difference matters because the two tokens ask different things of a reader: vendor-silent reads as closed until better documents appear, needs-drawing reads as an errand somebody can run today. The correction came from asr9k-cards, who had just been wrong in exactly this direction about the XFP - concluding a figure was unsourceable after searching the intake rather than the standards - and found it in INF-8077i ten minutes after looking somewhere else. IEC 61169-8 is the somewhere else here, and nobody has opened it yet.
gaps.wanted: a std/din-1-0-2-3 part and its standards.yaml key. THE CONNECTOR IS STANDARDISED, so a sourced dimension exists to be found rather than estimated - DIN 1.0/2.3 is specified in IEC 61169-8, and any manufacturer's bulkhead-jack panel drawing carries the D-hole figure. std/mcx is the worked example of exactly this being done properly earlier tonight: registered from IEC 61169-36 / CECC 22220 at 4.95 x 4.50 with confidence verified, replacing an estimate that was 28 percent too small. This should be done the same way, and until it is, an sma or smb standing in would be a plausible wrong answer - which is the failure mode this project keeps having to dig back out

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9006 Router - the 10RU, six-slot member of the ASR 9000 Series Aggregation Services Routers. Cards mount HORIZONTALLY: slots 0 and 1 at the bottom of the cage are reserved for a redundant RSP pair, slots 2 to 5 above them take line cards. Two fan trays sit above the cage behind a hinged door, and a single power shelf below it carries the AC or DC power modules, whose inlets are on the rear face. Modelled as a BARE CAGE: every slot is a bay that a card component drops into, not a traced faceplate.

gaps.note: cisco/a9k-power-module@1 states 142.78 mm wide. Three of them need 428.34 mm and this chassis's power shelf interior measures 416.50, so they do not fit - lint L13 flagged the overlap directly when they were placed at the measured centres. Against that, the stencil's shape box for the 'A9K Power Module' master reads 0.5477 in, which is 139.12 mm at the stencil's 1:10 scale, and my own measurement of the three openings in the ASR 9006 front master gives 138.35, 137.50 and 138.23. Those two agree to under a millimetre, and three at 139.12 come to 417.36 against a 416.50 shelf - the arithmetic a shelf that holds exactly three ought to produce. The 142.78 is most likely the art measured over something that is not the module's seating width, the same class of error as reading a card's shape box instead of its art. The bays here are sized to the measured openings, so the chassis is right and the component and the chassis disagree by about 3.7 mm until someone re-measures the master.
gaps.wanted: a re-measurement of the 'A9K Power Module' stencil master, or a Cisco dimension for the version 1 power module

gaps.note: NINE CARDS SHARE THESE SIX SLOTS AND TWO FAMILIES DISAGREE BY 32.8 mm ON THE ONE AXIS THAT HAS TO FIT ONE OPENING. The line cards and the blank filler are 395.7 mm; all four RSP-880 variants are 428.5. The measured cage opening is 352.59. The line-card story is coherent: a9k-slot-cover's own art measures a PLATE of 362.24 inside a 395.7 envelope, so the plate covers the 352.59 opening with 4.8 mm of overlap per side and the ejector brackets account for the remaining 16.7 per side. Every number has a job. The RSP-880's does not. 428.5 needs 37.96 mm of overlap per side to cover the same opening, and a card centred on this cage reaches x 22.99 to 451.49 in a 444.5 mm chassis - 6.99 mm PAST the outer wall, which is visible in the 3D view as the card's end standing proud of the side of the box. WHERE 428.5 COMES FROM, AND WHY IT IS THE SUSPECT: the RSP-880 data sheet's 'Physical specifications' row. This library's own a9k-rsp880-se provenance already records that NINE RSP AND RP MASTERS IN THE STENCIL ARE ONE DRAWING, scaled to four different stated widths - 402.8, 428.5, 428.2 and 403.4 - so "the drawing is generic across the family and cannot be all four sizes". The cage, by contrast, is measured off this chassis's own master and independently supported by Figure 19. NOT RESOLVED HERE. Two numbers describing different things is the likeliest reading - the same trap as a plate against an envelope - but nothing we hold says WHICH thing 428.5 measures, and inventing a smaller one would be the reconciliation this project keeps digging back out.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco mechanical drawing of an RSP-880 faceplate, or one measurement across a real card from ejector tip to ejector tip. Either settles it for all four variants at once and for every chassis they go in. REQUESTED FROM THE LAB, 2026-08-26, and tracked as roc-ops/ndv#16 - that issue carries the three conflicting Cisco figures and what to do when the number arrives.

gaps.note: NARROWED, not closed. This file and the ASR 9010's carried pitches that disagreed - 46.60 here against 44.33 there - for two chassis that take the same cards. Cisco's RSP-880 sheet resolved the 9010 half: the card is 46.0 mm thick and Cisco names the 9010 among the chassis it serves, so a 44.33 slot is impossible there and that cage is now divided on published card thicknesses. THIS CHASSIS IS NOT DISCRIMINATED BY THAT EVIDENCE. Its 279.63 mm cage admits both readings: four line card slots at 41.4 plus two RSP slots at 46.0 is 257.6, leaving 22.03 for guides; and an even six-way division at 46.60 is also >= 46.0 and so also admits the RSP-880. The even division is kept because it is what the cage measures and because nothing here favours the other, but it is an assumption and the 9010 shows the family does not always divide evenly. Neither this master nor the 9010's prints slot labels or draws cage dividers, which is why both were assumptions in the first place - the 9904, 9906, 9910, 9912 and 9922 all have a ruler in the picture and these two do not.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned front elevation of the ASR 9006, or a per-slot width from any Cisco document

gaps.note: Two figures in b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf give the ASR 9006 body width differently. Table 13 "Cisco ASR 9000 Series Routers Physical Descriptions" (p130) says 17.50 inches (44.45 cm). Figure 9 "Cisco ASR 9006 Router Chassis Footprint Dimensions - Top Down View" (p24) dimensions the same body at 17.38 inches (44.15 cm). Same measure, same part, 3 mm apart, so this is a real conflict and not two scopes. The manifest carries 44.45 because the spec table is authoritative for overall dimensions and because Cisco's own Visio master independently records 1.9 in at 1:10 over the flanges, which back-solves to Table 13's split once the 19.05 mm flange protrusion is subtracted. The likeliest reconciliation is that 17.50 is over the outer skin and 17.38 is the sheet metal at the section plane Figure 9 cuts, but no document we hold says that, so it is not written as though one does. The height is unaffected - both sources and the stencil agree on 17.50 in there.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco mechanical drawing with a tolerance, or a tape measure on a real ASR 9006

gaps.note: The power modules load from the front but their inlets are on the rear, and the only artwork we hold for that rear panel is the stencil's ASR-9006-AC Rear master, which draws the VERSION 1 tray: three IEC inlets labelled M2, M1, M0 left to right (mirrored from the front's M0, M1, M2) with the legend "100-240V 50/60 Hz 16A MAX (3X)" and a yellow warning label. This chassis is modelled as version 2, which has four modules and therefore four inlets, and no figure in any document we hold shows the version 2 rear panel. Rather than mirror three inlets into four and invent a pitch, the rear carries the inlet panel's outer band only. The DC rear is a further unknown again - there is no ASR-9006-DC master in the stencil at all.
gaps.wanted: a figure or photograph of the version 2 AC rear panel, and of the DC rear panel

gaps.note: The air filter is real, sourced and correctly typed as a bay - Table 17 of b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf places it along the right side accessible from the rear, and Figure 207 shows the panel and its thumb screw. What is NOT sourced is its geometry. Figure 207 is a three-quarter perspective view with no dimension lines on it, so its aspect is foreshortened and it fails gate 1 as a source of absolute size. The filter's 52 mm width and its 8 mm standoff from the rear edge are read as fractions of that figure and anchored to the chassis depth, and its height is set to the card cage band rather than measured. Treat the filter's extent as the one feature here that a tape measure would most likely move. Its presence, its side, its access direction and the fact that it is user-replaceable are all stated in words by the guide and are not in doubt.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned side elevation of the ASR 9006, or the air filter's own spare-part drawing

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9010 Router - the 21RU, ten-slot member of the ASR 9000 Series Aggregation Services Routers. Cards mount VERTICALLY across the full width of the cage: the two CENTRE slots, 4 and 5, are reserved for a redundant RSP pair, with four line card slots either side of them. A cable management tray runs along the top, two stacked fan trays and a front air intake sit below the cage, and two power shelves fill the bottom. Modelled as a BARE CAGE: every slot is a bay a card component drops into, not a traced faceplate.

gaps.note: THESE BAY DIMENSIONS WERE GROWN TO MEET A COMPONENT AND ARE NOT MEASUREMENTS. Each was set by taking the size of a card the bay accepts, because a fit check reported the bay as too small. On this chassis: 403.10 on 8 bays - the 5th-generation envelope, 403.10 long 406.40 on 2 bays - a9k-rsp, 406.40 long The danger is specific and it is why they are listed rather than left to look like geometry. A fit check compares a bay to a component and NEITHER of them to the world, so it is satisfied by both being wrong together exactly as easily as by both being right. Every mismatch resolved by moving one side removes the signal without adding any truth, and once resolved nothing will flag it again. These are the entries where that happened, so the record survives the check going quiet. What IS independently grounded and is not in this list: the cage extents, measured off the stencil and confirmed on several chassis by printed slot labels or a card guide rail; the slot pitch; the 395.70 fourth-generation envelope, which is Cisco's own "includes ejector bracket/lever" figure; and the shapesheet sizes for the power modules and fan trays. The ejector arithmetic that explains why a bay legitimately exceeds its cage opening - 355.60 against 395.70, 40.10 mm - is also sourced, and it justifies the SHAPE of these numbers without justifying any particular one of them.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned figure giving the clear opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would replace every reconciled figure above with a measured one

gaps.note: A THIRD LINE OF EVIDENCE ON THE ~428 mm CONTROL CARDS, derived rather than asserted, and it comes from parts that have nothing to do with the question. The vertical space available to a card is bounded by whatever structure sits above and below its cage, and on this chassis that space measures the figure recorded in card-envelope-headroom below. A card envelope larger than that cannot be installed whatever any data sheet says, because something else is already there. Applied across the family: ASR 9010 399.96 mm between the cable management tray and the card guide bar ASR 9910 421.79 mm between the tray band and the front air intake ASR 9922 420.30 mm between the tray band and the fan band ASR 9912 439.21 mm - does NOT exclude 428.5, so this chassis is silent on the question ASR 9906 unbounded above in the model, so no constraint is derivable Three of the five independently exclude a 428.2-428.5 card. That is a separate argument from the slot pitch and from the ejector arithmetic, and it agrees with both. THE 9912 DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT and is recorded as silent rather than as agreement - a constraint that fails to bite is not evidence either way, and reporting it as if it were would manufacture support. gaps.wanted: a figure dimensioning the clear vertical opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would turn all of this from derived to measured

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9910 Router - the 21 RU, ten-slot member of the ASR 9900 generation. The bays for 10 to 19 are geometrically identical to 0 to 9 and carry no rotation, because the card is inverted about its own long axis rather than rotated in the plane of the panel - a `rotate: 180` would spin the faceplate end for end, which is a different thing and would put the ejectors at the wrong ends.
